title: Impact of Compulsory Schooling on Wages

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
Method chosen: Two-Stage Least Squares (Instrumental‐Variables).

Why IV?  
Education (x) is potentially endogenous: unobserved ability, family background, or reverse causality may bias the OLS estimate of schooling on wages (y).  Compulsory‐schooling legislation (z) generates exogenous variation in education that can be exploited as an instrument.

Key assumptions  
1. Relevance – the instrument affects education: Cov(z, x) ≠ 0 (checked with the first-stage F-statistic).  
2. Exclusion – compulsory-schooling laws influence wages only through schooling, not directly nor through omitted channels (after conditioning on controls).  
3. Monotonicity – no individual obtains less schooling because the compulsory law becomes stricter.  
If (1)–(3) hold, the 2SLS estimator recovers the causal Local Average Treatment Effect of an additional year of compulsory schooling on log-wages.

## 2. R Code
```r
############################################
# Impact of compulsory schooling on wages  #
############################################
# Load packages
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(readr)      # fast data import
  library(AER)        # ivreg
  library(sandwich)   # robust vcov
  library(lmtest)     # coeftest
  library(dplyr)      # data manipulation
})

# 1. Read the data
dat <- read_csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s68_data.csv",
                col_types = cols())

# Simple sanity check
print(head(dat, 3))

# 2. OLS benchmark (possibly biased)
ols <- lm(y ~ x + controls, data = dat)
cat("\n--- OLS estimate ---\n")
print(coeftest(ols, vcov = vcovHC(ols, type = "HC1")))

# 3. IV estimation (2SLS)
iv <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls, data = dat)
cat("\n--- IV estimate (2SLS) ---\n")
print(coeftest(iv, vcov = vcovHC(iv, type = "HC1")))

# 4. First-stage relevance check
first_stage <- lm(x ~ z + controls, data = dat)
cat("\nFirst-stage F-statistic on instrument (z):\n")
fs_test <- waldtest(first_stage, . ~ controls, vcov = vcovHC(first_stage, type = "HC1"))
print(fs_test)

# 5. Weak-instrument diagnostics (Cragg-Donald / Stock-Yogo)
cat("\nDiagnostics from summary(iv, diagnostics = TRUE):\n")
print(summary(iv, diagnostics = TRUE))

# 6. Reduced-form (effect of z directly on y)
rf <- lm(y ~ z + controls, data = dat)
cat("\nReduced-form (effect of z on y) ---\n")
print(coeftest(rf, vcov = vcovHC(rf, type = "HC1")))

# 7. Robustness: specification without controls
iv_nocontrol <- ivreg(y ~ x | z, data = dat)
cat("\nIV without controls ---\n")
print(coeftest(iv_nocontrol, vcov = vcovHC(iv_nocontrol, type = "HC1")))

# 8. Report core causal estimate cleanly
beta_iv <- coef(iv)["x"]
ci_iv   <- confint(iv, vcov = vcovHC(iv, type = "HC1"))["x", ]
cat("\n==============================\n")
cat(sprintf("Causal effect of one extra year of schooling on log-wage (IV): %.4f\n", beta_iv))
cat(sprintf("Robust 95%% CI: [%.4f, %.4f]\n", ci_iv[1], ci_iv[2]))
cat("==============================\n")
```

## 3. Expected Findings
Economic priors and the existing literature (e.g., Angrist & Krueger 1991) suggest a positive return to schooling.  
• Sign: Positive.  
• Magnitude: Around 0.08–0.12 in log points per additional year (≈ 8–12 percent higher wages), possibly larger than OLS if OLS is downward-biased by measurement error in education.

Thus we expect the IV coefficient on education (x) to lie in the 0.08–0.12 range, pass the relevance test with a first-stage F-statistic > 10, and robustness checks to yield qualitatively similar positive estimates.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Use compulsory schooling year as an instrument for education.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The analysis suggests that additional compulsory schooling has a negative impact on log wages.
